title: Advancing Education through Tutoring Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how tutoring systems have evolved from early computer-assisted instruction to modern AI-driven Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) and Robot Tutoring Systems (RTS), and what that evolution means for learning, engagement, and ethics in education. The authors ask three main questions: which technological breakthroughs enabled personalized tutoring, how current systems use real-time adaptation to improve engagement and academic performance, and what ethical challenges have emerged alongside these technologies. The review is motivated by persistent global learning gaps and interest in AI-based tools that can personalize instruction at scale.

The study uses a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of 86 representative studies selected from an initial pool of 340 records spanning 1972 to 2024. The authors analyze tutoring systems through a four-part framework covering artificial intelligence, system behavior, engagement, and affordances. They also conduct a latent class analysis that groups systems into three categories: computer-based ITS, robot-based verbal tutoring systems, and multimodal tutoring systems that combine verbal, visual, and physical interaction. Across the reviewed studies, key AI techniques include Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, natural language processing, and large language models.

The population context is broad rather than tied to a single sample, because this is a review of prior studies across educational settings. The included literature spans multiple learner groups, with examples and discussion prominently involving younger learners, middle school mathematics students, secondary physics learners, and some higher-education contexts. The review focuses primarily on students as end users of tutoring systems in educational environments, rather than on teachers or administrators as the main participants.

The main conclusions are that tutoring systems show strong promise for improving learning outcomes, personalization, and student engagement, but different forms have different strengths. Computer-based ITS are more scalable and cognitively adaptive, while robot-based systems are stronger for social and emotional engagement. The authors argue that hybrid systems integrating both approaches may offer the greatest educational benefit. They also conclude that important challenges remain, especially around scalability, data privacy, bias, transparency, and the still-limited cognitive adaptability of robotic systems.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: Intelligent Tutoring Systems are software-based AI tutoring systems that provide adaptive, personalized instruction, feedback, and content adjustment based on student performance.
identified_tools.use_case: This systematic literature review synthesized evidence on computer-based tutoring systems as one major class of tutoring systems, alongside robot tutoring systems and multimodal systems, across 86 studies from 1972–2024.

findings.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, software-based ITS were synthesized as showing significant improvements in academic achievement and learning outcomes, with strong cognitive adaptability enabled by techniques such as Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and LLMs. The paper does not report a pooled effect size, confidence interval, or a single aggregate sample size for ITS-only outcomes.
findings.measure: Academic achievement and learning outcomes across reviewed ITS studies

findings.finding_summary: The review found that ITS are highly scalable relative to robot-based systems because they rely on existing computer infrastructure and can be cloud deployed with minimal hardware requirements. This is presented as a comparative systems-level advantage rather than a quantified effect estimate.

identified_tools.name: Robot Tutoring Systems (General)
identified_tools.description: Robot Tutoring Systems are AI-supported tutoring systems embodied in physical robots that use verbal, gestural, and social interaction to support learning and engagement.
identified_tools.use_case: This systematic literature review synthesized evidence on robot-based tutoring systems as a major tutoring-system class, focusing on their engagement, motivation, adaptability, and ethical considerations across the included literature.

findings.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, robot tutoring systems were consistently synthesized as improving student motivation, emotional engagement, and social interaction through verbal encouragement, gestures, and human-like behaviors. The review emphasizes these benefits especially for younger learners, but does not provide a pooled effect size, confidence interval, or aggregate sample size.
findings.measure: Motivation, emotional engagement, and social interaction outcomes

findings.finding_summary: The review reports promise for RTS in supporting learning outcomes, but also states that the direct cognitive impact of robotic systems remains an area for further exploration and is less advanced than software-based systems in cognitive adaptability. No pooled effect size or RTS-specific aggregate sample size is reported.

identified_tools.name: Multimodal Tutoring Systems (General)
identified_tools.description: Multimodal tutoring systems combine multiple interaction modes, such as verbal, visual, text, and physical/robotic interaction, to create adaptive and immersive tutoring experiences.
identified_tools.use_case: This review identified multimodal tutoring systems as a third latent class, integrating AI-driven adaptation with verbal, visual, and physical interaction modes.

findings.finding_summary: The review characterizes multimodal tutoring systems as excelling in engagement and adaptability by combining verbal, visual, and physical interaction with advanced AI techniques. Their educational benefit is described qualitatively, but no pooled learning-effect estimate, confidence interval, or aggregate sample size is reported for this class.
findings.measure: Engagement, adaptability, and learning outcomes in multimodal tutoring systems

quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review of 86 studies using PRISMA with explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria and synthesis procedures, but it does not report pooled meta-analytic effect sizes and synthesizes heterogeneous systems at the category level.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally positive impacts on learning, engagement, and motivation across tutoring-system categories, but the magnitude of effects is unclear because no pooled effect sizes or confidence intervals are provided.
